slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.

slides.direction: "A pull request is a GitHub object that stores two names, a base and a head, and everything it shows is computed from three commits: the tip of the base, the tip of the head, and their merge base."
quotes: A pull request is a GitHub object that stores two names, a base and a head, and everything it shows is computed from three commits: the tip of the base, the tip of the head, and their merge base.
slides.caption: The page changes when one of the three changes, and for no other reason.

lines.s: # On the server. Opening pull request 1 for feature/priority-routing, as Git data:
# Clients may read refs/pull/ but not write it:
# A clone fetches refs/heads/* only, so the pull request ref is not in Asha's clone:
16d4788 Fix the name of the escalations queue
! [remote rejected] pr-1 -> refs/pull/1/head (deny updating a hidden ref)
error: failed to push some refs to '../../server/ticket-router.git'
! [remote rejected] main -> refs/pull/9/head (deny updating a hidden ref)
error: failed to push some refs to '../../server/ticket-router.git'
# On the server. A merge without a working tree (Chapter 8, section 8.17):
merge=$(git commit-tree $tree -p main -p refs/pull/1/head -m "Merge refs/pull/1/head into main")
| * 16d4788 Fix the name of the escalations queue
# The test merge commit is on neither branch:
# What a CI job sees when it checks out the merge ref:
HEAD is now at 135aad1 Merge refs/pull/1/head into main
# On the server, after one more commit landed on main:
# The merge ref is a stored commit. It is as fresh as its first parent.

# No clean tree, so no test merge commit and no refs/pull/2/merge:
# The head branch is deleted. The pull request ref still names the commits:
16d4788 Fix the name of the escalations queue

slides.direction: The two tabs.

lines.s: | * 16d4788 Fix the name of the escalations queue
# The "Commits" tab: commits reachable from the head branch and not from the base branch.
16d4788 Fix the name of the escalations queue
# The "Files changed" tab: merge base compared with the head. Three dots.
# Two dots compare the two tips. The newer commit on main appears, reversed.
# A three-dot diff is a two-dot diff whose left side is the merge base.
git diff --stat $(git merge-base origin/main feature/priority-routing) feature/priority-routing
# After the base branch is merged into the head branch, the tip of main is the merge base.
16d4788 Fix the name of the escalations queue

slides.lead: You should now be able to say:
items: A pull request is a GitHub object over two names; the page is computed from the base tip, the head tip and their merge base.
GitHub writes refs/pull/N/head and, when the merge is clean, a test merge under refs/pull/N/merge, in the base repository.
CI for a pull request tests the test merge, which is stored and can be stale; with a conflict there is none.
"Commits" is git log base..head; "Files changed" is git diff base...head.
Merging the base into the branch makes the two-dot and three-dot diffs equal and adds a merge commit to the list.

beats.text: CI, the automatic testing of every change, was green on the pull request, your proposal to merge a branch into main. Ten minutes after the merge it was red on main. Nobody pushed anything in between except the merge itself. Your CTO asks: what did CI test?
beats.tele: CI, the automatic testing of every change, was green on the pull request, your proposal to merge a branch into `main`. Ten minutes after the merge it was red on `main`. Nobody pushed anything in between except the merge itself. Your CTO asks: what did CI test?

beats.text: It tested a commit, one saved snapshot of the project, that is on no branch and in nobody's clone: a test merge that GitHub made, of your branch with main as main was at that moment. main moved on before you merged, and the test merge was not regenerated.
beats.tele: It tested a commit, one saved snapshot of the project, that is on no branch and in nobody's clone: a test merge that GitHub made, of your branch with `main` as `main` was at that moment. `main` moved on before you merged, and the test merge was not regenerated.

beats.text: To answer questions like this one you need to know exactly what a pull request is made of, and which three commits every part of its page is computed from. Keep that green check in mind. In the demo you'll watch it go stale.

beats.text: In one sentence: opening a pull request moves no branch. It creates a GitHub object and a little Git data in the base repository: a read-only ref for the head commit and, when the merge is clean, a test merge commit. The base is the branch you merge into, here main. The head is the branch whose commits you offer. A ref is a name that holds a commit ID.
beats.tele: In one sentence: opening a pull request moves no branch. It creates a GitHub object and a little Git data in the base repository: a read-only ref for the head commit and, when the merge is clean, a test merge commit. The base is the branch you merge into, here `main`. The head is the branch whose commits you offer. A ref is a name that holds a commit ID.

beats.text: You should be able to say which layer owns each item.
beats.tele: You should be able to say which layer owns each item.

beats.text: Your commits, the head branch, the base branch: Git. Objects and refs in the head and base repositories.
beats.tele: Your commits, the head branch, the base branch: Git. Objects and refs in the head and base repositories.

beats.text: The pull request number, title, description, labels, reviewers, reviews, comments, review threads: GitHub's database, not in any clone.
beats.tele: The pull request number, title, description, labels, reviewers, reviews, comments, review threads: GitHub's database, not in any clone.

beats.text: refs/pull/<number>/head: Git data written by GitHub. A ref in the base repository, read-only for you.
beats.tele: `refs/pull/<number>/head`: Git data written by GitHub. A ref in the base repository, read-only for you.

beats.text: The test merge commit and refs/pull/<number>/merge: Git data written by GitHub. A commit and a ref in the base repository, "when possible".
beats.tele: The test merge commit and `refs/pull/<number>/merge`: Git data written by GitHub. A commit and a ref in the base repository, "when possible".

beats.text: Checks and commit statuses: GitHub and Actions, attached to commit IDs in GitHub's database.
beats.tele: Checks and commit statuses: GitHub and Actions, attached to commit IDs in GitHub's database.

beats.text: The "Commits" and "Files changed" tabs: GitHub, computed from the three commits, stored nowhere in Git.
beats.tele: The "Commits" and "Files changed" tabs: GitHub, computed from the three commits, stored nowhere in Git.

beats.text: GitHub's reference says: "When you open a pull request, GitHub creates temporary Git references that point to the pull request's head branch and, when possible, to a simulated merge result." The page no longer spells out the ref names. Two other pages of the documentation confirm them: the checkout instructions and the Actions documentation.
beats.tele: GitHub's reference says: "When you open a pull request, GitHub creates temporary Git references that point to the pull request's head branch and, when possible, to a simulated merge result." The page no longer spells out the ref names. Two other pages of the documentation confirm them: the checkout instructions and the Actions documentation.

beats.text: The test merge. GitHub "creates a merge commit to test whether the pull request can be automatically merged into the base branch. This test commit is not added to the base branch or the head branch". Its parents are the latest commit on the base branch and the pull request's head commit. In our picture that's 135aad1.

This test commit is not added to the base branch or the head branch". Its parents are the latest commit on the base branch and the pull request's head commit. In our picture that's `135aad1`.

beats.text: Three facts about it. First, CI uses it. For a pull_request event, the Actions documentation states that the checkout action "checks out the merge branch. Your CI tests run against the merged result, not just the head branch alone".
beats.tele: Three facts about it. First, CI uses it. For a `pull_request` event, the Actions documentation states that the checkout action "checks out the merge branch. Your CI tests run against the merged result, not just the head branch alone".

beats.text: Second, it is a stored commit, so it can be stale: main moves on, and its parent is still the old tip. The version note: before the nineteenth of February 2026, the test merge commit was also regenerated when somebody viewed the pull request page.
beats.tele: Second, it is a stored commit, so it can be stale: `main` moves on, and its parent is still the old tip. The version note: before the nineteenth of February 2026, the test merge commit was also regenerated when somebody viewed the pull request page.

beats.text: Since then, it is generated only when changes are pushed to the pull request branch, when the merge base changes, or when the current test merge commit is older than 12 hours. Do not build automation on the freshness of the merge ref.
beats.tele: Since then, it is generated only when changes are pushed to the pull request branch, when the merge base changes, or when the current test merge commit is older than 12 hours. Do not build automation on the freshness of the merge ref.

beats.text: One caveat marked unverified in the book: a REST guide still says the commit "is created when you view the pull request in the UI". That conflicts with the later changelog, which the course follows.
beats.tele: One caveat marked unverified in the book: a REST guide still says the commit "is created when you view the pull request in the UI". That conflicts with the later changelog, which the course follows.

beats.text: Third, when the merge conflicts, there is no merge ref. Two documented consequences: the merge button is deactivated until the conflict is resolved, and workflows will not run on pull_request activity. A pull request with no CI run at all is often a conflicting pull request.
beats.tele: Third, when the merge conflicts, there is no merge ref. Two documented consequences: the merge button is deactivated until the conflict is resolved, and workflows will not run on `pull_request` activity. A pull request with no CI run at all is often a conflicting pull request.

beats.text: Two more properties. The head ref outlives the head branch: delete the branch, and the commits are still one fetch away. Nobody can rewrite or delete these refs with Git. And the base is pinned: GitHub "sets the base to the commit that branch references" when you open the pull request, and does not update that commit when the branch moves. That is why the pull request page and a compare page of the same branches can show different diffs.
beats.tele: Two more properties. The head ref outlives the head branch: delete the branch, and the commits are still one fetch away. Nobody can rewrite or delete these refs with Git. And the base is pinned: GitHub "sets the base to the commit that branch references" when you open the pull request, and does not update that commit when the branch moves. That is why the pull request page and a compare page of the same branches can show different diffs.

beats.text: Now the second question, with both branches on screen. In one sentence: the "Commits" tab is the output of git log base..head, and the "Files changed" tab is the output of git diff base...head, a diff from the merge base to the head. The merge base is the most recent commit that both histories contain: here, 9a383e5.
beats.tele: Now the second question, with both branches on screen. In one sentence: the "Commits" tab is the output of `git log base..head`, and the "Files changed" tab is the output of `git diff base...head`, a diff from the merge base to the head. The merge base is the most recent commit that both histories contain: here, `9a383e5`.

beats.text: You learned both notations in the history videos. For git log, A..B means "reachable from B and not from A". For git diff, which compares two snapshots, A...B means "from the merge base of A and B to B". GitHub's documentation states which one it uses: "Pull requests on GitHub show a three-dot diff", and gives the reason: "it focuses on 'what a pull request introduces'".
beats.tele: You learned both notations in the history videos. For `git log`, `A..B` means "reachable from B and not from A". For `git diff`, which compares two snapshots, `A...B` means "from the merge base of A and B to B". GitHub's documentation states which one it uses: "Pull requests on GitHub show a three-dot diff", and gives the reason: "it focuses on 'what a pull request introduces'".

beats.text: The limit of the three-dot diff, as a one-line root cause from the textbook: a three-dot diff is not "what will change on main when I merge". It is "what the head changed since the merge base". The two differ exactly when both sides changed the same thing. The test merge is the object that answers the first question.
beats.tele: The limit of the three-dot diff, as a one-line root cause from the textbook: a three-dot diff is not "what will change on `main` when I merge". It is "what the head changed since the merge base". The two differ exactly when both sides changed the same thing. The test merge is the object that answers the first question.

beats.text: Quick quiz. main gained a commit after you branched. Does the "Files changed" tab show that commit's change? A: yes, reversed. B: no. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. `main` gained a commit after you branched. Does the "Files changed" tab show that commit's change? A: yes, reversed. B: no. Your answer?

beats.text: B. Three dots start at the merge base, so later commits on main stay out. A is what two dots show, and the demo proves it.
beats.tele: B. Three dots start at the merge base, so later commits on `main` stay out. A is what two dots show, and the demo proves it.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy: a pull request is a change request clipped to two bookmarks in a shared book. The form, who asks, who must sign, the discussion, lives in the office's filing system.

beats.text: The analogy breaks at one point that matters. The office also keeps a copy of the proposed pages in its own drawer under your request number, where you can read it and cannot change it, and where it stays after you remove your bookmark.

beats.text: That drawer is refs/pull/N/head. It is the reason a deleted branch is not a deleted commit.
beats.tele: That drawer is `refs/pull/N/head`. It is the reason a deleted branch is not a deleted commit.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Believing CI tested the head commit. Root cause: for a pull request event the checkout is the test merge, a stored commit that can be older than the base branch.
beats.tele: Believing CI tested the head commit. Root cause: for a pull request event the checkout is the test merge, a stored commit that can be older than the base branch.

beats.text: Deleting a branch to remove a pushed secret. Root cause: refs/pull/N/head still names the commits, and nobody can delete that ref with Git.
beats.tele: Deleting a branch to remove a pushed secret. Root cause: `refs/pull/N/head` still names the commits, and nobody can delete that ref with Git.

beats.text: Comparing with git diff main and concluding that GitHub shows something else. Root cause: that is a two-dot diff of the tips; the page shows a three-dot diff from the merge base.
beats.tele: Comparing with `git diff main` and concluding that GitHub shows something else. Root cause: that is a two-dot diff of the tips; the page shows a three-dot diff from the merge base.

beats.text: Reading the "Files changed" tab as "what will change on main". Root cause: it is what the head changed since the merge base; the two differ when both sides changed the same thing.
